passage: Dear Rukmini, I have to tell someone. In yesterday's seminar on the water project, everyone looked so certain. Even our professor said the budget looked fine. But I noticed that the maintenance cost was left out of the sheet. I kept my hand down. I thought: they are all clever, they must have counted it, and I would look silly. Afterwards, on the stairs, Meenal said, "Did nobody notice the maintenance line?" and Aakash said, "I did, but I thought I was missing something." Half of us had the same doubt and said nothing! I want to bring it up next week. Wish me courage. — Yamini

qa.q: What was left out of the budget sheet?
qa.a: The maintenance cost was left out of the sheet.

qa.q: Why did Yamini keep a hand down in the seminar?
qa.a: Everyone else looked certain, so Yamini assumed the others knew better and feared looking silly; the feeling was doubt turned into self-silencing.

qa.q: What turning point does Yamini choose after the stairs conversation?
qa.a: Yamini decides to bring the maintenance question up next week, having learned that others held the same doubt.

qa.q: What might Aakash have been thinking when saying "I thought I was missing something"?
qa.a: Aakash probably assumed the group must have a reason and that the doubt showed a gap in Aakash's own understanding, so silence seemed safer than asking.

grounding: A student keeps a reservation private because everyone looks certain, not realising several others are silent for the same reason.

passage: Deepak, it's me, Sunaina. Remember the pitch review last week? The whole room was nodding. The slide said two hundred sign-ups, and I had this tiny voice saying that number looks made up. But everyone looked so sure, even Vikram, who is the sharpest of us. So I decided I was the one who did not understand. I stayed silent and even nodded. After the meeting Rina said in the lift, "I thought the number looked odd too," and then Kunal said, "Me too!" I nearly laughed. Three of us had swallowed the same doubt for an hour. Deepak, I am going to say something at the next one, even if my voice shakes.

qa.q: How many sign-ups did the slide claim?
qa.a: The slide said two hundred sign-ups.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina decide to be silent and even nod in the meeting?
qa.a: Sunaina thought everyone else looked sure, so the doubt must be Sunaina's own misunderstanding; it was self-doubt more than agreement.

qa.q: What choice does Sunaina make at the end of the story?
qa.a: Sunaina decides to say something at the next review even if the voice shakes, having learned that others had the same doubt.

qa.q: What might Kunal have felt when saying "Me too!" in the lift?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt relief and surprise at finding out the doubt was shared, after an hour of holding it alone.

grounding: A student keeps a doubt to themselves because everyone else looks certain, not realising others are silent for the same reason.

passage:
In the college chemistry lab, the four of them bent over the titration results. Ojas tapped the notebook. “Concentration is 0.5. Clear. Let's write it up.”
Lavanya looked at her burette readings again. She had got 0.3, twice. But Ojas sounded so sure, and Farah and Nitin were already nodding. They must know something I missed, she thought. She kept her notebook closed.
They submitted 0.5.
The next week the lab assistant returned the reports. “Correct value was 0.3,” he said. Ojas groaned. Farah said, “I got 0.3 too! I thought I'd done it wrong.” Nitin said, “Same.”
Lavanya stared at them. All three of them had been sitting on the same doubt.

qa.q: What value did Ojas say the concentration was?
qa.a: He said the concentration was 0.5.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya keep her notebook closed?
qa.a: She felt unsure of herself and assumed the others knew better, because Ojas sounded so certain and the others were nodding.

qa.q: What could the group try before submitting next time?
qa.a: Each person could read out their own result first, before anyone announces an answer, so different values come out.

qa.q: How might Farah feel when she learned her 0.3 was right?
qa.a: Farah might feel frustrated and a bit foolish for doubting that result, and relieved not to be the only one.

grounding: Shows a student keeping a doubt to herself because others looked certain, not realising others were silent for the same reason.

passage:
Dear Pema,
Remember how I used to argue about everything? Not any more, apparently.
Our drama club voted yesterday to do the long historical play for the fest. Three hours, forty costumes, six weeks. Samar pitched it and everyone looked thrilled. I had this small voice saying, we can't possibly finish this. But Samar is brilliant, and everyone seemed so sure. I assumed they'd worked it out.
So I raised my hand with the rest.
The funny part? Even Rafiq, who argues with Samar about everything, just sat there with his arms folded. He didn't say a word. Neither did Jyoti. I didn't think about it then.
Anyway, rehearsals start Monday. Wish me luck.
Gargi

qa.q: How many costumes does the play need?
qa.a: It needs forty costumes.

qa.q: Why did Gargi raise her hand with the rest?
qa.a: Gargi felt doubtful but hesitant, assuming the others had worked it out because everyone seemed so sure.

qa.q: What would you advise Gargi to do now?
qa.a: Gargi could quietly ask Rafiq and Jyoti what they thought, since their silence hints they had doubts too.

qa.q: How might Pema read the bit about Rafiq?
qa.a: Pema, knowing Gargi well, might notice Rafiq's unusual silence and guess he had doubts too, even if Gargi hasn't seen it.

grounding: A student writes of keeping a doubt private because everyone else looked certain, without noticing others were silent too.

passage:
So you want the full story of the trek? I'm Parul, and I'm still a little embarrassed.
Our mountaineering club met to plan the monsoon trek. Mridul's cousin had suggested a route along a ridge. The seniors said, “Great, done.” Everyone nodded.
I'd read that this ridge gets slippery in the rain, with a closed section. But nobody else said anything, so I figured they'd checked. They're the experienced ones, right?
Two days before we left, I finally messaged Mridul. He replied in one second: “I read the same thing! I thought I was being silly.” Then Tanu said she'd had the same worry. Then Jasmine.
Four of us. All quiet. We changed the route that evening, thank God.

qa.q: Who suggested the route along the ridge?
qa.a: Mridul's cousin suggested it.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: Parul felt doubtful and unsure, assuming the experienced seniors must have checked, so Parul stayed quiet.

qa.q: What small step changed the plan?
qa.a: Parul's message to Mridul opened the door, and once one doubt was said aloud, the others shared theirs too.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt when Parul's message arrived?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved, since he'd had the same worry but thought he was being silly.

grounding: A student keeps a safety doubt private because others seem certain, then learns several others were silent for the same reason.

passage:
Monday: At the study-group table in the library, Karan announced the plan. Each of them would teach one chapter the night before the exam. Everyone nodded. Baljeet thought, one night isn't enough for five chapters. But Lakshmi looked calm and Karan sounded certain, so Baljeet assumed they'd done this before and kept quiet.
Thursday: At chai, Lakshmi stirred her cup for a long time. "Can I say something? I don't think the one-night plan works." Baljeet nearly laughed with relief. "I thought the same on Monday." Mitesh looked up. "So did I. I thought you all knew better."
Saturday: The three of them asked Karan for ten minutes. Karan listened, frowned, then admitted, "Honestly, I wasn't sure either." They moved the teaching sessions to a week before the exam.

qa.q: On which day did Lakshmi first say the doubt aloud?
qa.a: On Thursday, at chai.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet stay silent on Monday?
qa.a: Baljeet felt unsure and assumed the calm, certain faces meant the others knew better, so the doubt seemed too small to raise.

qa.q: What habit could the group use to catch doubts earlier?
qa.a: End each plan with a quick round where everyone names one worry, so silence is not mistaken for agreement.

qa.q: What does Karan's "I wasn't sure either" tell us about Karan's side of it?
qa.a: Karan sounded confident but was privately unsure too, and was probably relieved that someone finally questioned the plan.

grounding: Shows a student keeping a doubt private because everyone looks certain, later finding several others were silent for the same reason.
